Chapter 8: Rebuilding Trust—Reconciliation, Forgiveness, and the Limits of Healing.
If justice was tough, reconciliation was even tougher. Imagine trying to live side by side with people who, not long ago, might have wanted you dead. How do you start to trust again when betrayal had become almost normal?
Let me tell you about a woman who came back to her village after years spent in exile. Her house was still there, just as she'd left it. But everything else? It felt different. Her old neighbors greeted her, but with those awkward, uncertain smiles—you know the kind where no one’s quite sure what to say. She tried to rebuild her life—planting a fresh garden, fixing up the roof, sending her kids back to school. But the memories hung on, and forgiveness? That didn’t come so easily.
Then, in another part of the country, there was a man who’d confessed what he’d done during the gacaca courts. He worked quietly in the fields, kept his head down, and avoided the faces of those he’d hurt. He wanted to make things right, he really did, but he just didn’t know where to start. The guilt weighed on him, and the road to redemption seemed impossible to find.
Still, some communities found ways to break through those barriers. They organized projects together—digging wells, fixing up roads, planting trees. Side by side, people started seeing each other not as enemies, but as neighbors again. It wasn’t quick or easy. The journey had setbacks, but every now and then, there were moments of real kindness and hope.
Picture this: a local pastor gathers survivors and perpetrators for weekly meetings. At first, everyone’s tense. There’s anger, suspicion, and a whole lot of silence. But gradually, things begin to shift. People start listening. They hear each other's stories, they pray, and—little by little—they begin to see the humanity in one another. Suddenly, forgiveness doesn’t seem so far-fetched.
Of course, not everyone could forgive. Not everyone wanted to. For some, the pain was just too deep, the loss too big. But even trying to reconcile was a victory in itself—a way to say, “Hatred doesn’t get the last word.”
The government pushed a new vision—one of national unity. They wanted everyone to see themselves, not as Hutu or Tutsi, but as Rwandans. Schools introduced new lessons, all about shared identity and working together for a better future. The message was simple: you can’t change the past, but the future? That’s still open.
Yet, none of this was easy or guaranteed. Old resentments simmered just out of sight, and the fear of more violence never really disappeared. So, rebuilding trust became a daily effort—an ongoing process of choosing to believe in something better, even after everything had been shattered.
